Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Akua had always been drawn to helping others, which is why she became a counselor at a local community center. But her own life took a drastic turn during her tour of duty in a combat zone two years ago. She was part of a team that provided medical aid to civilians in a war-torn village when their convoy came under attack. In the chaos, Akua found herself separated from her unit and pinned down behind a crumbling wall as helicopters thundered overhead, spewing gunfire and debris everywhere. The sounds of those helicopters still haunted her. Even now, whenever she heard the distant whir of aircraft or saw one flying low in the sky, she felt like she was back in that village, frozen with fear, unsure if she'd make it out alive. Akua had come to dread going outside on windy days when the sounds carried farther, and she often found herself checking the weather forecast obsessively, bracing for those dreaded noises. But it wasn't just the helicopters that triggered her memories. Family gatherings had become a minefield too. Her relatives would make innocent comments about how proud they were of her service or ask about her time overseas, unaware of the pain their words stirred up in Akua. She began to avoid family events and stopped attending social functions with friends from before the war. What frightened her most was that she couldn't shake the feeling that somehow, there was something fundamentally wrong with her – a flaw that had led to the traumatic event itself. As time went by, these feelings of inadequacy seeped into other areas of Akua's life. She stopped pursuing new relationships or friendships, fearing that others would see through her façade and discover the 'real' her – someone broken and no longer capable of doing the things that defined her as a person. She even found it challenging to watch TV programs or films featuring combat scenes, feeling an overwhelming sense of anxiety whenever the sounds or images brought back memories. Akua's work at the community center began to suffer too. Her usual empathy and patience were replaced by irritability and restlessness, especially when clients came in with their own trauma stories. She couldn't bear the thought that someone else might be going through what she had endured – it only reinforced her self-comparison: 'somebody else would not have gotten into this situation.' The pressure to maintain a professional demeanor while secretly feeling so damaged began to take its toll, and Akua eventually took an extended leave of absence. Despite her best efforts, the isolation didn't bring Akua any solace. She felt like she was losing herself in the darkness, just as she had during those terrifying hours pinned behind that wall. The recent anniversary of the event had passed, stirring up emotions Akua thought she'd long buried. What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with an old friend who'd also been deployed – someone who understood what it meant to be broken and struggling to put the pieces back together. Akua is now taking tentative steps towards confronting the demons that have haunted her for so long, fearful of what she might discover about herself but more afraid of living in this limbo forever.
